label: Uneasy thaw
summary: The world moves up to 48 — still 'Mixed / uneasy', but the top of that band — because the single largest source of global risk this summer stepped back a further pace on Monday. President Trump said negotiations with Tehran would begin today, a day after he called off the planned strike on Iran's energy infrastructure, and Iran's foreign minister said talks with Oman on managing the Strait of Hormuz were in their final stages; President Masoud Pezeshkian called the Islamabad Memorandum the 'centre of gravity' of Iran's future foreign relations. Markets took the point immediately. WTI opened below 80 dollars and Brent slid toward the same level, well off the 90.17 Brent close of 31 July; Dow futures rose 265 points, the Sensex opened 788 points higher, and fuel-price caps came down across Fiji, Samoa and Tonga — diesel off 13.7 percent in urban Viti Levu — the first real cost-of-living relief the Pacific has had since April. Separately Japan and the United States confirmed their first coordinated currency intervention since 2011, buying yen on Friday after the currency hit 40-year lows; it recovered 1.4 percent to 155.20, though the Nikkei fell and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington 'would not hesitate' to intervene again. None of that reaches the wars still running. Israeli forces killed at least 17 Palestinians in Gaza, among them Abdullah Abu Taif, 33, his pregnant wife Abeer Anan, 29, and their five-year-old son Azzam in an air raid on the Al-Sousi Tower in western Gaza City, days after the Board of Peace published its disarmament-and-withdrawal roadmap. Russian and Ukrainian strikes killed fourteen people between them, nine of them in Russia — including a thirteen-year-old near a playground in Belgorod — and five in Ukraine, with Zelensky again warning he has no Patriot interceptors left. In Ethiopia, federal forces and the TPLF exchanged artillery and drone fire near Sheraro in the most serious breach yet of the Pretoria agreement; the fighting stopped by Sunday evening but analysts called it the gravest incident since 2022. The climate ledger is the worst part of the day. Three fires around Spokane, Washington — Old Trails, Autumn Lane and Fairview — destroyed more than 600 structures across 5,390 acres at zero containment, put roughly 65,000 people under evacuation orders and drew a state wildfire emergency; Mayor Lisa Brown called it 'really the worst natural disaster our region has faced.' South Korea recorded its hottest temperature since observations began, 42.5C at Yangsan on a fifth consecutive day above 40C, while Japan issued heatstroke alerts for 30 of 47 prefectures and wildfires burned in Greece, Spain, France, Tunisia, Algeria and Morocco. Cuba's grid collapsed into another nationwide blackout. Spain's Ceuta death toll reached 72 after some 60,000 people crossed from Morocco, and Indonesian rescuers were still searching for 41 people missing from the ferry Mutiara Sentosa 2, which burned off Madura with 271 aboard. Against that, an international team published in Nature the first all-optical photonic time crystal, halving terahertz photon losses. The headline matches the rubric formula with no editorial adjustment.

drivers.headline: President Trump says negotiations with Tehran will begin Monday, a day after he cancelled the planned strike on Iran's energy infrastructure, while Iran's foreign minister says talks with Oman on managing the Strait of Hormuz are in their final stages and President Masoud Pezeshkian calls the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding the 'centre of gravity' of Iran's future foreign relations; Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tehran is now more prepared to negotiate over its nuclear programme and the strait, though US forces remain on full alert and almost no terms have been published

Israeli forces kill at least 17 Palestinians across Gaza despite the Board of Peace roadmap that Trump has called a 'monumental step' toward peace, including three killed in an air raid on a residential apartment in the Al-Sousi Tower in western Gaza City — Abdullah Abu Taif, 33, his pregnant wife Abeer Anan, 29, and their five-year-old son Azzam, according to medical sources at al-Shifa Hospital; Israel has not publicly accepted the latest proposal and Hamas says it will implement nothing until Israeli forces withdraw as agreed

Russian and Ukrainian strikes kill fourteen people between them: Ukrainian drones kill nine inside Russia, including three hit in a vehicle in Udmurtia, two in a residential building in Engels and four in Belgorod region among them a 13-year-old near a playground, with the Saratov oil refinery and the Engels airbase among the targets; Russian strikes kill five in Ukraine in Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk and Kherson, after a barrage of 220 aerial weapons in which air defences downed 154 drones but only one ballistic missile because, Zelensky says, there are no Patriot interceptors left

Ethiopian federal forces and the TPLF exchange heavy artillery and drone fire near Sheraro in western Tigray close to the Sudanese border in what analysts call the most serious breach yet of the three-year-old Pretoria agreement, with Tigray's regional government in Mekelle saying federal troops opened the assault at dawn and federal minister Abraham Belay saying the TPLF started it and calling for dialogue; the fighting stopped by Sunday evening but the TPLF had already declared the Pretoria deal 'effectively dead' in mid-July and analysts warn of escalation without outside intervention

Crude falls sharply and equities rally on the decision not to strike Iran: WTI opens below 80 dollars a barrel and Brent slides toward the same level, well off the 90.17 dollars Brent closed at on 31 July, as OPEC also adds supply; India's Sensex opens 788.7 points higher at 78,883.34 and the Nifty adds 189.1 points to 24,572.70 with 2,288 stocks advancing to 458 declining, while Dow futures rise 265 points ahead of the US July jobs report — though Asian trading is mixed, with the Nikkei down 1.04 percent and Shanghai off 0.59 percent

Japan's finance ministry confirms it conducted a coordinated yen-buying intervention with the US Treasury on Friday — the first joint US-Japan currency action since 2011 — after the yen slid to 40-year lows; the currency jumped 1.4 percent to 155.20 per dollar, a near three-month high and a 3.8 percent gain over two sessions, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent saying Washington 'would not hesitate to participate in further joint intervention' and Trump saying 'they wanted a little bit of help, and we're always there for Japan'; the rapid appreciation knocked the Nikkei lower

Cuba's national grid fails again, plunging the island into another nationwide blackout announced late Sunday, with the Electric Union not immediately identifying a cause; the grid collapsed three times in July alone, leaving roughly ten million people without power for stretches that disrupted hospitals, water supply, transport and communications, and the government blames the US oil blockade imposed on 3 January that cut off Venezuelan fuel while critics point to decades of underinvestment in plants now more than thirty years old

Three fast-moving fires around Spokane, Washington — the Old Trails fire north of Airway Heights, the Autumn Lane fire near Five Mile Falls and the Fairview fire near Mead, together designated the Spokane Complex — destroy more than 600 structures across 5,390 acres at zero containment and put roughly 65,000 people under evacuation orders, with entire blocks in the Indian Trail and Five Mile Prairie neighbourhoods reduced to foundations; a state wildfire emergency has been declared, no injuries have been reported, and Mayor Lisa Brown called it 'really the worst natural disaster our region has faced'

South Korea records its highest temperature since observations began — 42.5C (108.5F) at Yangsan at 1:26pm on Sunday, a fifth consecutive day above 40C in the city and above a 41.4C mark set at the same station on 31 July — with more than twenty localities under the emergency heatwave alerts introduced this year; Japan issued heatstroke warnings for 30 of its 47 prefectures, wildfires driven by heat and wind burned in Greece, Spain and France and across Tunisia, Algeria and Morocco, and a dangerous heatwave gripped the western United States

Spain puts the Ceuta death toll at 72 after roughly 60,000 people crossed from Morocco into the North African enclave between Thursday and Sunday, five more bodies having been recovered along the coastline on Sunday alone; more than a thousand people have needed medical treatment, over 48,000 of those who crossed returned to Morocco within 48 hours, the Civil Guard is identifying the dead by fingerprint and DNA, Madrid has installed a 500-metre floating barrier, and 22 EU member states have asked for coordinated border action while Italy has temporarily suspended Schengen free movement with Spain

At least five people are dead and 41 unaccounted for after the passenger ferry Mutiara Sentosa 2 caught fire between 6am and 7am on Sunday in waters off Madura island while sailing from Surabaya in East Java to Makassar in South Sulawesi with 232 passengers and 39 crew aboard; 225 people were pulled from the water by nearby vessels, the Indonesian navy sent a warship and a rescue vessel from Surabaya to join the search, and the cause of the fire is not yet known

An international team from École Polytechnique, the Collège de France, Thales' Laboratoire Albert Fert and Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf reports in Nature the first experimental all-optical photonic time crystal, using a micrometre-scale gold plasmonic metamaterial driven by HZDR's TELBE superradiant terahertz source to modulate a material's optical properties on picosecond timescales and cut terahertz photon dissipation by roughly half — a result that moves photonic crystal control from space into time and opens routes to ultrafast optical computing, new telecommunications systems, terahertz lasers and medical imaging
